mninuerido.c: MNINUERIDO. is a Word Hequettly used in Writs, Declarations and Pleadings; and its Ute is only to declare and ascertain the Person or Thing which was nained or left doubtful before.

maculaepatica.c: MACULA Epatica, is a Spot of a brown or of a fad yellow Colour, about an Hand's Breadth broad, chiefly seizing upon the Groins, the Breast'and Back, nay, sometimes it covers the whole Body; is attended with a certain flight sipereeer the Skin, which lets fall Scales, or a sort of Dendriff from it, which yet do not stick all together, but are disseminated here and there, and sometimes disappear, sometimes break out again. " Blanchard.

maculssolares.c: MACULS Solares; fee Spots in the Sun.

maculavolatica.c: MACULA Volatica, is a red or purple Spot here and therein the Skin; which, if it touch any Orifice in the Body, as the Mouth, Nostrils, Eyes, Ears, sc. and pierce so far, it becomes mortal: It is often fatal to Children. Blanchard.

madrierinfortification.c: MADRIER, in Fortification, is a thick Plank arm'd with Plates. of Iron, and having a Con cavity fafficient to receive the Mouth of the Petard when charged, with which it is applied against a Gate, or any thing else that you design to break down. This Term is also appropriated to certain flat Beams, which are fixed at the Bottom of a Moat, to support a Wall. There are also Madriers lined with Tin, which are covered with ath, to serve as a Defence against artificial res.

magdaleones.c: MAGDALEONES, are Pieces of Plaister made up in Form of a Cylinder, or long Roll.

magicksqxare.c: MAGICK Sqxare, is when Numbers in Arith'metick Proportion are disposed into such parallel and equal Ranks, as that the Sums of each Row, as well diagonally, as laterally, shall be all equal. s 10) 3 Thus these Nine Numbers, 2, 3) 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10, being disposed into this square Form, they do every way, di - reftly and diagonally, make Eighteen.

magisteryaword.c: MAGISTERY, a Word used by the Chymifts, sometimes for very fine Powders, made by Solution and Precipitation of the Matter; as Magistery oO! Bifinuth, Lead, &c.. And sometimes tis made to figuifie Reins and Resinous Extrads. Thus the Reins. of Jalap, Scamniony, & c. are called Ma gif teries.; Mr. Boyle takes the true Notion of a Magi / very to be a Preparation of Body ( norman Analysis of it, for the Principles are not separated) whereby the whole, or very near the whole of it, by some Additament, is turned into a Body of a different kind; as when Iron or Copper is turned into chrystals of Mars or Venus, &c. The canting Alchymitfts talk also of the magistery of the Philosopher's Stone, which will be worth enquiring into, when they will tells us what the Stone it self is. For an Instance how they are made, I will mention two or three, Magistery of Bismuth, is made by dissolving the Bismuth in Spirit of Nitce, and pouring upon it salt Water, which will precipitate the Magistery ro the Bottom in a white Powder. Magiflery of Lead, is made by dissolving Sac charum Saturni in distilled Vinegar; and then precipitating ic with Oil of Tartar, made per deliquium. Ref; alap, Tarbieh Magistery or Refine of Scammony, Falap, Turbith, & e. techale hy a Dissolution of eed in Spirit of Wine; acid then precipitating it by common Water, or Water impregnated with a little Alum, And after these manners are most other Magis teries made.

magnacharta.c: MAGNA Charta, was granted the ninth Year of Henry the third, and confirmed by Edward the Fir The Reason why it is termed Magna Charta, was either i it contained the Sum of of all the Liberties of England, or else because there was another Charta, called Charta de Fore fta, established with it, Which was the less of the two; or because it contained more than many other Charters, or more than that of King Henry the First, or of the great and remarkable Solemnl tithe deubiieing Excommunication, and direful " Avathemas again. the Infringers of ic. Pie " tte tells us, that King Pia to appease his Barons, yielded to Laws or Articles of Govern'ment mitch like to this Great Charter; but we have now no ancient er Law written than this, which was thought to be so beneficial to the Subject, and a Law of so great Equity, in comparison of those which were Pornely in use, that King Henry for the granting of it had the fifteenth Peny of all the moveable Goods, of both Temporal ity and earner; od

magnet.c: MAGNET. Sturnius in his Epi / tola Invitatoria Dat. Al tors. 1682. observes that the attrap tive Quality of the Magnet hath been taken Notice of beyond all History: But that it was our Countryman Roger Bacon who first discovered the Verti city of it, or its Property of pointing towards the Pole, and this about 400 Years since. The / ta - ians first discovered, that it would communicate this Virtue to Steel or Iron. The various Declination of the Needle under different Meridians, was first discovered by Sebaftian Cabo tt; and its Inclination to the nearer Pole by our Countryman Robert Norman. The Variation of the Declination, o that tis not always the same in one and the same Place, he observes, was taken notice of but a few Years before, by Hevelius, Auzout, Petit, Volckamer and others. The Properties or Phenomena of this wonderful Stone, as they have been discovered by Gilbert, aes Cab eus, Des Cartes, and others, are these: 1. That in every Mag wer there are two Poles, one pointing North, the other South; and if a Stone be cut or broken into never so many Pieces, there are these two Poles in each Piece, 2. That these Poles in divers Parts of the Globe, ate diversly inclined towards the Earth's Centre. 3 - That these Poles, tho contrary to one another, do help mutually toward the Magnet's Attraction and Suspension of Iron. 4. If two Magnets are spherical, one will turn or conform it self tothe other, so as either of them would do to the Earth; and that after they have so conformed or turn'd themselves, they endeavour to approach to join each other; but if placed in a contrary Position, they avoid each other. s. If a Magnet be cut thro the Axis, the Parts or Segments of the Stone, which before were joined, will now avoid and fly each other. 6. If the Magnet be cut by a Se tion perpendicular to its Axis, the two Points which before were conjoined, will become contrary Poles, oneinone, - the other in the other Segment. Wey 7. Iron receives Virtue from the Magnet by Application to it, or barely from. an Approach near it though it doth nor touch it; and the Iron receives this Virtue variously, according to the Parts of the Stone tis made to touch, or made approach to.; 8. If an oblong piece of Iron. be any how ap - plied to the Stone, it receives Virtue from it only as to its Length. 9. The Magnet loses none of its own Virtue by communicating any to the Iron, and this Virtue it can communicate to Iron very speedily; tho the longer the iron touches or joins the Stone, the longer will its communicated Virtue hold; and averter Magnet will communicate more of it and sooner than one not so good. EHO 10. Thar Steel receives Virtue from the Magnet better than Iron. 11. A Needle touch'd by a Magnet will turn its Ends the same way towards the Poles of the World, as the Magnet will do it. " 12. That neither Loadstone nor Needles touch'd by it, do conform their Poles exa tly to those of the World, but have usually some Variation from them: And this Variation is different in divers Places and at divers times, in-the same Place. 13. That a Loadstone will take up much more Tron when arm'd or cap'd, than it can alone: And that tho an Iron Ring or Key be suspended by the Loadstone, yet the magnetical Particles do not hinder that Ring or Key from turning round any way either to the right or left.: 14. That the Force of a Loadstone may be variously increased or lessened by the various Application of Iron, or another Loadstone to it. 1 s. That a strong Magnet, at the least Distance from a lesser or a weaker, cannot draw to it a piece of Iron adhering a tually to such lesser or weaker Stone; but if it come to touch it, it can draw it from the other: But a weaker Magnet or even a little Piece of Iron, can draw away or separate a Piece of Iron contiguous to a greater or stronger Loadstone.. 16. That in our North Parts of the World, the South Pole of a Loadstone will raise up more Iron than the North Pole.: 17. That a Plate of Iron only, but no other bo -. dy interposed can impede the Operation of the Loadstone, either as to its attractive or dire give Quality. Mr. Boy / e found it true in Glasses sealed hermetically; and Glass is a Body as impervious as most are to any Effluvia. 18. That the Power or Virtue of a Loadstone may be impaired by lying long in a wrong Posture, as also by Rutt, Wer, & c. and may be quite destroyed. by Fire, H

magneticalamplitude.c: MAGNETICAL Amplitude, is an Arch of the Horizon, contained between the Sun at his Rising or Setting, and the East and Weft Point of the Compass: Or it is the different Rising or Setting of the Sun from the East or Weft Points of the Compass; and is found by observing the : bi at his Rising or Setting, by an Amplitude Com - ate.

magneticalazimuth.c: - MAGNETICAL Azimuth, is an Arch of the Horizon, contained between the Sun's Azimuth Circle, and the Magnetical Meridian: Or it is the apparent Distance of the Sun from the North or South Point of the. Compass; and may be found by observing the Sun with an Azimuth Compass, when he is about 10 or 15 Degrees high, either in the Forenoon or Afternoon.

magnifie.c: MAGNIFIE, is a Word used chiefly in reference to Microscopes; which are usually said to magnify Obje & ts, or to make them appear bigger than, they-really are.; - But in ie Microscopes do not, nor can at all " er. any Obje t, but only thew more of it to the Eye than before was taken Notice of, as will be apparent from the following Considerations. For, Sirt, Tis clear that the Images of all Objects which are represented or pictured on the Retina in the Bottom of our Eyes, ( and by which way all Vision is made) those Images, fay, must of necessity be very mall, in Proportion to the Obje ts themselves; as is demonstrable to any one's Reason, that will confider the Smallness of the Fundus Oculi; and to his Senses, that will but take the Pains to try the Cartesian Experiment, of putting a Bullock's Eye in the Hole of a darkened Room. ( Vid. Cart. Diope. cap. 5.) Now there being no Reason to suppose, that che bare Communication of that Pi ure to the Brain by the Optick Nerve, or Animal Spirits, can magnifie it again, so as to equal it with the Obje & ts themselves; it must and doth - follow, that we always have Things represented to us less than they are, in the common way of Vision. 2. mercuriusdulcis.c: MERCURIUS Dulcis, or Sweet Sublimate of Maca by the Chymiits sometimes called Aguila Alba, is thus made. Sixteen Ounces of Sublimate Corrosive being powder'd in a Glass, or Marble Mortar, ( for it must be never done in a Metalline one) - is mixed by little and little with Twelve Ounces. of Mercury revived from Cinnabar, ( or put Mercury:) The Mixture is stirred about with a Wooden Pestle, till all the Crude Me: disappear; then it is put into a Matrass, two Thirds of which remain empty: The Vessel is heated in Sand, gently at but afterward the Fire is increased to the Third Degree: In four or five Hours the Sublimate will stick to the Top and Neck of the Dials: Fling all away that is'not White, and then powder that, and sublimate it again, and a Third time, if you would have it very white. Thus is. the strongest Poison, perhaps in Nature, corre - & ed into a very gentle and useful Medicine, by adding more Mercury to it. The Reason of which seems to be, That by these new Sublimations, the Corroding Acids of the Sublimate have their Points broken, and perhaps some of them loaded with the Addition of more Mercury, and so can't a & t with the same deleterious Force as they did before.

Tis call'd Meridian, because when the Sun cometh to the South Part of this Circle, " tis then Meridies, Mid-day, or High-noon; and then the Sun hath its greatest Altitude for that Day, which therefore is called the Meridian Altitude. These Meridians are various, and change according to the Longitudes of Places; fothat they may be said to be infinite in Number, for that all Places from East to Weft have their several Meridians: But there is ( or should be) one Six'd, whith is called the First Meridian.

meridionalparts.c: MERIDIONAL Parts, miles, or minutes, in Navigation, are the Parts by which the meridians in Mr. Wright's Chart ( commonly, though falsely, called Mercator's) do increase as the Parallels of Latitude decrease: And the Co-fine ofthe Latitude of any Place being equal to the Radius or Semi-diameter of that Parallel, therefore in the true Sea Chart, or Nautical Plani - sphere, this Radius being the Radius of the Equinoctial, or whole Sine of 90; the merid io -. nal Parts at each Degree of Latitude must increase, as the Secants of the Arch contained be-tween that Latitude and th Equinoctial do increase. The Tables therefore of meridional Parts, which you hav in Books of Navigation; are made by a continual Addition of Secants They are calculated in some Books ( as in Sir onas Moor's Tables) for every Degree and Minute of Latitude; and these will re either to make or graduate a Mercator's Chart, or to work the Mercator's Sailing. To use them, you must. enter the Table with the Degree of Latitude at the Head, and with the minute on the first Column towards the left Hand; and in the Angle of meeting you will have the meridional Parts.. ine a i: Having the Latitudes of two Places, to find the meridional Miles or minutes between them, confider whether the Places be'one under the Equinoctial and the other wide thereof; or the one on the one side of the Equinoctial, and the other on the other; or whether they both lie on the same side: For, according to these Positions, there's a Threefold Cafe.; ba x 1. moments.c: MOMENTS, are sometime taken for the Jeaft and most insensible Parts of Time; as when we fay, such a Thing was done in a Moment. In Mathematicks, Moments are such indeterminate and instable Parts of Quantity, as are supposed to be in perpetual Flux, 7.. either continually decreasing or increasing; which latter are taken for Affirmative and Positive Moments, and the former for Negative or Subtra table ones; And these continually increasing or decreasing Particles are supposed to be infinitely mall; for as soon as ever they come to be of any finite Magnitude, they cease to be moments. Moments therefore are to be look'd upon as the generative Principles of finite magnitudes; and are here supposed to have no Magnitude, but to be Inceptive only of it, to use Dr. Wallis's Word. And because tis the same thing, if inthe room of these moments, the Velocities of their Increases or Decreases be made use of, or the finite Quantities proportionable to such Velocities; this method of proceeding, which considers the Motions, Changings or Fluxions of Quantities, hath come to be called Fluxions. Moments also in a Physical Sense, as they are used in reference to the Laws of motion, signify the Quantities of motion in any moving Bodies; and sometimes, simply, the motion it self; and they define it to be the Vis infita, or Power by which any moving Bodies do continually change . their Places. And in comparing the motions of Bodies, the Ratio of these moments is always compounded of the Sa Hers matter in, and the Celerity of the moving Body: So that the moment of any moving Body may be consider'd as a Ret fangle under the Quantity of Matter into the Celerity. ae one 3 certain ace equal pa ave their Sides reciprocal ion able, ( 14. . 6. Eucl.) therefore if the dia ee any see ables are equal, the Quantity of matter in one, to that of the other, will be reciprocally:: as the Celerity of the latter to the Celerity of the former: And vice versa, if the Quantities of matter are reciprocally proportionable to the Celerities, the moments or quantities of motion in each will be equal. The moment of any moving Body may be considered also as the aggregate or Sum of all the moments of the Parts of that Body; and therefore where the magnitudes and Number of any Particles are the same, and where they are moved with the same Celerity, there will be the same moments of the Wholes.

monochord.c: MONOCHORD, a kind of Instrument anciently of singular use for the regulating of Sounds; but some wade the Name of Monochord to an Instrument that hath only one single String, as the Trumpet Marine. The Ancients made use of the Monochord to determine the Proportion of Sounds to one another: When the Chord was divided into two e - ual Parts, so thar the Terms were as 1 and 1, they called them Unifons; but if they were as 2 to, they called them Of saves or Diapafons 5 when they were as 3 to 2, they called them Fifths, or Diapentes; if they were as 4 to 3, they called, them Fourths, or Diatefferons; if the Terms were as 5 to 4, they call it Diton, or a Tierce major; but if the Terms were as 6 to 5, then they called it a Demi-diton, or a Tierce minor 5 and lastly, if the Terms were as 24 to 25, they called it a Demit on or Die ze. The Monochord being thus divided, was properly that which they called a Sy / tem, of which there were many kinds, according to the different divisions of the Moncchord.

month.c: MONTH, properly speaking, is the Time in which the Moon runs through the Zodiack, and therefore is accounted by the motion of the Moon; and therefore the Lunar Month is either Periodi - which. is. the Time of the Moon's motion t ng more than 29 Days and annals,; . There is also. a Solar Month, which is the Time that the Sun takes up in running thro " one of the Signs of the Zodiack, and is almost so Days and Half. nd both these Solar and Lunar Months are either A ( tronomical, like those above-mention'd; or Civil, which are various, according to the Usage of accounting in different Places, Cities and Nations. The Egyptians account by Solar Months, each of 30 Days; and to compleat their Year, after x 2 such months, they added 5 days, which the odd Hours made up. But most of the ancient Nations accounted the Lunar Syncdical Month; as the Fews, Greeks, and the Romans, till 7. Cefar's Time; and as the Mahometans do to this day. And because these months did not contain an exa t Number of days, to adapt them to Civil Computation, they accounted alternately one month to have 30, and the next 31 days; and by this means they made two such Civil months to be equal to two Lunar ones of 29 days and half; and they brought it to ass, that the New month, fora Run of many ears, did not much deviate from the sirt da of the Civil Month. i

moor.c: MOOR at Sea, signifies the ag the Anchors of a Ship so, as is best and fafeft for her Riding. There are several ways of Mooring a Ship. Sometimes they moor her a thwart, b laying one Anchor on one side of a River, an another right against it on the other side; in order to make both the Cables bear together, as well at Tide of Ebb, as at Flood. To moor Aooglt, is to lay one Anchor right in the middle of the stream, and another right a head of the ship, which is done when they are in danger of driving shoar; for by this means both her Anchors a bear together, and so will save h r from falling on either shore. To moor Water sot, is to moora Ship in the middle between the two former ways, quartering; as it were, neither across the Tide, nor along it, but between both. When a ship comes into a Place of Riding, the master and his mates observe on what Point of the Compass the Wind is likelieft to endanger the ship, and there they lay out an Anchor; and this is called mooring for East, North, &c. according to the Point the is moored upon. They don't fay a ship is moored, unless she have at least two Anchor's out; except in one Cafe, and that is, when, tho she have but one Anchor out, yet there is a Hawser shoar; and then they fay she is moored with her Head to the Shoar.

mosaicwork.c: MOSAIC Work, was anciently used only in Pavements, and began in Rome about Sylia'stime; who made Pavement of Mofaick Work at Pre - nest in the Temple of Fortune, about 170 Years before Christ. It was call'd Lithoftroton, in Greek, only a Stone Pavement; but it is under tood of Figures made or represented by inlaying of small Stones, or rather pieces of Stone of different Colours; by the Variety of which, many curious Figures may be wrought. Afterward it came to be in Fashion for the Inside of the Walls of Rooms; and now adays they work it with Shells, or mall Pieces of Glass variously colour'd and figur'd: " Tis a very pleasant and lasting Ornament, when " tis curiously and excellently done.
MOSAIC Work, is corruptly so called 5 it should be'Mufaick; in Latin mufivum Opus, and sometimes tis called also Pavimenta Teffilace.

MOTION: From the first of Sir If, Newton's three Laws of Motion or Nature mentioned under this Word Motion in Vol. I. by way of Corollary may be inferred, ( 1.) That no Particle of Matter, or any Combination of such ( that is, no Body whatever) can either move of it self, or alter the Direction of its Motion, because tis entirely passive and indifferent as to Motion or Reft; so that neither Motion or Reft are essential to Matter. ( 2.) Tis plain also from hence, that naturally of it self, no Body can ever move in a Curve Line; for since all Motion is originally and naturally rectilinear, tis, impossible that any Body can move in a Curve or Line that is not strait of it self; because then it must of it elf continually alter the Direction of its Motion, which cannot be, by the former Corollary; wherefore the Motion of the Heavenly Bodies in Circles or Ellipses cannot be accounted for by the natural Laws of Motion; bur it is owing to the Will of the great Creator wae they are kept in their Orbits by an attractive force. From the second of the three Laws of Motion, it follows, that all Effects will always be proper. tional to their Adequate Causes 3 and thesis a - 7 Degree of any Force will produce any Degree of Motion, a double Degree of the same Force will produce a double Degree of Motion, a Triple, a Triple, and so on in any Ratio whatsoever. And this Motion must proceed on in the same Direction with that of the moving Force, because tis from That only that the Motion arises; and Bodies once in Motion, cannot change their Direction of themselves. Dr. Chirac, professor of medicine at Montpellier, supposes, and thinks he can prove it analytically, that every muscle being composed of a vast multitude of fibres, like threads, folded up all together, within one kin or membrane, and every fibre having its proper-vein, artery, and nerve, it hath also from pace to pace several little Cavities or Pores which are of an oblong Form, when the muscle is slack or flaccid; but the blood circulating pte the muscle, is continually disposing into those Pores a sulphurous recrement, abounding with A / kali Salts, which meeting with the Spirits that flow also by the Nerves into those oval Pores, their Nitro-aerial particles ferment in a most violent manner with the saline ones of this sulphurous recrement, and thereby distend the pores so, as to make them change their long oval figure into a round one; and thus the muscle must be contracted.

musclevein.c: MUSCLE Vein. This Vein is two-fold, the Superior and the Inferior. The former arises from the muscles of the Neck, and the latter from the upper muscles of the breast; and this sometimes opens into the external Jugular.

musculusstapidis.c: MUSCULUS Stapidis, isa muscle of the ear, which lies hid in a bony Pipe, excavated in the Os Petrofum, almost at the bottom of the Tympanum, whence it takes its Origin. Its belly is big and fleshy, and suddenly forming a very thin Tendon, which descends to its insertion at the head of the Scapes: When this ats, it draws the Stapes upwards, to the Foramen Oval.

mylohoideus.c: MYLOHOIDEUS, is a muscle which Fad lo - pi us makes double, - but Mr. Cowper thinks it a single one, not being to be divided without great Violence: It possesses all that pace which is between the lower Jaw, and the Os Hyoides; arising fleshy from both sides of the Mandible Internally, near the Dentes Molares; whence marching with a, double Order of fleshy Fibres, the out - ward most of which pass dire tly to their Implantation in the Os Hyoides; and the middle run transversely over the following muscles, being inseparably joined to each other with a middle Line, as is well exprest by Bidloo, ( Tab. 14) Besides the Uses commonly ascribed to this muscle in moving the Os Hyoides, Tongue, and Larynx upwards, and forwards, and to either side; its last described tran verse order of Fibres, have still further use in compressing the Glandule Sublinguales, which lie immediately under them on each side; whereby they hasten the egress of the Spittle, Rosi the inferior salival Duds in the Mouth, Hence it is we employ these muscles ( as in the action of Deglurition) when we want Saliva to moisten the Mouth: And in that action also they supply it with fresh Saliva, to join with those aliments where mastication is not required 5 which artifice of Nature deserves our Admiration. Newton, that Light is propagated inTime; and he then fed about 10 Minutes were taken up in its Pafge from the Sun to us: But in his Opticks he determines this Matter more accurately. Romer first, and after him others, had observed that the ar fes of Jupiter's Satellites happen about 7 or 8 Minutes sooner than they ought to do by the Tables, when the Earth is interposed between the Sun and that Planet; but as much later, when the Earth is ond the Sun in pen of Jupiter: the Reason bch is, that the Light of the Satellites hath farther to go inthe latter Cafe, that in the former, by the Diameter of the Earth's Orbit. Some Inequalities of Time indeed may arise from the Eccentricities of the Orbits of the Satellites; but these can't answer in all the Satellites, and at all times, to the Position and Distance of the Earth from the Sun. The mean Motion of Supirer's Satellites is also winter in his Descent from his Aphelium to his Peribelinm, than in his Ascent in the other half of his Orb. But this Inequality hath refle t to the Position of the Earth, and in the three Interior Satellitesisinfenfible; as resound by Computation from the Theory of their Gravity. After this Sir I / Isaac advances this Proposition, which is the rath of Part 3. of the 2 d Book of his Opticks, viz. Every Ray of Light in its Passage thro any refracting Substance is ig into certain Transient Constitution or State, which in the Progress f the Ray returns at equal Intervals, and disposed the Ray at every Return to be easily transmitted thro " the next refracting Surface, and between the Returns to be easily reflected by it, This is manifest from his 5, 9, 12 and 15 th Observations. Whence it appears, that one and the same sort of Rays, at YS Angles of Incidence on any thin tran rent late, is alternately reflected and transmitted for many Success ions, according as the Thickness of the Plate increases in Arithmetical Progression of the Numbers o, 1, 2, 3941 5, 5, 7, 8, &c. ( See Colours.) And this alternate Reflection and Transmission, he found by his 24 th Observation, continues for above 100 Vicissitudes 5 nay, as he proves afterwards, to many thousands; being propagated from one surface of a Glass Plate to another, tho the Thickness of the Plate be 4 of an Inch and more. So that this Lic Alternation seems to be propagated from every reseating Surface to all - Dittasces without End or Limitation. He shews also, that this alternate Refle tion and Refraction d is on borb the Surfaces of every thin Plate, because it depends on their Distance 5 but that ir is performed at the second Surface. Ir is also influenced by some A tion or Disposition propagated from the spirit ro the second 3 because otherwise at the second it would not depend on the first And this A ion or Disposition, in its vit pel intermits and returns by equal Intervals, What kind of A tion or Difpolitien this is; whether it confit in a vibrating or a circulating Motion of the Ray, ot of the Medium, or something else, the Author does not st od But he allows those, that are averse to all new Discoveries which they can't explain by Hypothe les, at preterit to suppose, That as Stones by falling upon Water put it into an undulating Motion, and all Bodies by Percussion excite Vibrations in the Air; so the Rays of Light, by impinging on any refra ting or reflecting Surface, excite Vibrations in the refracting or reflecting Medium; and by so doing do agitate the solid Parts of the refra ting or reflecting Body, and by that Agitation cause the Body to grow warm or hot: That the Vibrations thus excited are propagated in the refracting or reflecting Me - diwm or Substance, much after the manner that Vibrations are propagated in the Air for. causing Sound; and that they move faster than the Rays, so as to overtake them; and that when any Ray is in that part of the Vibration which conspirer with its Motion, it easily breaks thro'a refra ing Substance; but when it is in'a contrary part of the Vibration, which impedes its Motion, it is easily reflected; and consequently, that every Ray is successively disposed to be easily reflected or. transmitted by every Vibration which overtakes it. Whether this Hypothesis be true or false he doth not confider at present, contending himself with the ge of the Salt, That he hath discovered the Rays of Light by some Cause or other to be thus alternately disposed to be reflected or refracted for many icidhtades. The Returns of this Disposition of any Ray to be refle ted, he calls Fits of esl Refiasions and those of its Disposition to be tran mi and the Space it puts between every Return and the next Return, he calls the Intervals of its Fits. Then at Prop. 13. he shews, that the Reason wh the Surface of all thick transparent Bodies reflect part of the Light incident on them, and refra t the reft, is that some Rays at their Incidence are in Fits of easy Reflection, and others in Fits of easy Tranfiniffion. This appears from his 24 th Observation; where the Light refle & ted by thin Plates of Glass and Air, which to the naked Eye appeared evenly white all over, did thro a Prism appear waved with many Success ions of Light and Darkness, made by alternate Fits of easy Refle & tion and easy Transmission; the Prism revering and distinguishing the Waves of which the white Light was composed. And hence tis plain, Light is in its Fits of easy Reflection and easy Transmission before its Incidence on any tran parent Body: And ere it is put into such Fits at its A Emiffon from Luminous Bodies, and continues in them during all its Progress. For these Fits are of a latin Nature; as appears by what he proves elsewhere. He egy? apes ited, he calls Fits of easy Tran / vision 5 - Fits, th Reason fraction, do refracti most " He supposes here the it Bodies to be thick; because if the Thi of the: be much less than the Interval of the Fits of easy Reflection and easy Transmission of the Rays, the: Body lofeth its reflecting Power. For if the Rays, which at their entring. into the Body are put into Fits of easy Transmission, arrive at the farthest ce of the Body, before they be out of those must be transmitted. And this is the Bubbles of Water lose their reflecting Power when they grow very thin, and why all Opake Bodies, when reduced into very Parts, become Transparent.: He thews also, that those Surfaces of ee rent Bodies, which, if the Rays be ina Fit of in sit of Refle tion, do it most easily. mortmainstatute.c: MORTMAIN Statute: There was a Statute made in 7 Ed. 1. de Terris in manum mort aam non is to restrain the Donation of any Lands or Tenements to Religious or Ules, where they lay in a Dead Hand, without Succession or due Service to the Lord and the King. After which Statute the Lands so given away were for - ited to the King, if the immediate Lord of the ee made not his Claim within Year after such Alienation. When the King by special Licence dispensed with the Statute of Mortmain, there was a previous Inquisition ad quod Damp num, and a Return upon Oath that it would be no Prejudice to the Dignity and Revenues of the Crown. This Law is now relaxed by Stat. 39 El iz. c, 5. of giving Lands to Hofpitals; and by 14 of Car. II. c. 9. about purchasing Lands and Tenements for the Poor within London and Westminster.
